channel.title: Daily Recap — 📟Tech News
channel.description: What happened in 📟Tech News, recapped daily from subscribed feeds.

item.title: An Illinois college tried to cancel its Flock contract — and Flock refused
item.description:
The Verge reports a college in Illinois tried to cancel its contract with Flock, the license-plate-reader camera company, and the company refused. It's a striking illustration of the power imbalance in surveillance-tech contracts.

Flock's cameras have spread rapidly across American towns and campuses. This story raises the obvious question: what recourse does a community have when it decides it no longer wants to be watched?

Sources

  • The Verge: A college in Illinois tried to cancel its Flock contact and it refused

item.title: Silicon Valley falls in line with Trump's attempt to rename AI
item.description:
The Verge reports Silicon Valley is falling in line with the Trump administration's attempt to rebrand artificial intelligence. The piece examines who's complying, who's resisting, and what a politically driven rename would even mean for an industry that already can't agree on what to call the technology.

It's the latest front in the ongoing collision between tech and Washington — and a reminder that AI's biggest battles are increasingly political, not technical.

Sources

  • The Verge: Silicon Valley is falling in line with Trump’s attempt to rename AI

item.title: NASA dumped 800GB of Artemis II data online
item.description:
NASA has published more than 800GB of Artemis II data online, The Verge reports — a massive open-data drop from the crewed lunar mission program.

It's a goldmine for researchers and space nerds alike, and a strong statement about open science: the data belongs to everyone, not just the agency that collected it.

Sources

  • The Verge: NASA dumped over 800GB of Artemis II data online

item.title: Learning to use local AI: exciting, overwhelming, frustrating
item.description:
The Verge dives into the world of local AI — running models on your own hardware instead of in the cloud. The verdict from the learning curve: exciting, overwhelming, and frustrating in roughly equal measure.

It's an honest accounting of where consumer local AI stands: powerful enough to be genuinely useful, rough enough that patience is still required.

Sources

  • The Verge: Learning to use local AI is exciting, overwhelming, and frustrating

item.title: Why the LeapPad couldn't survive the iPad
item.description:
The Verge looks back at the LeapPad — the kids' tablet that couldn't survive the iPad era. It's a sharp little business obituary about what happens when a general-purpose device eats a single-purpose one.

The pattern repeats across tech history, but the LeapPad story has a particular poignancy: it was genuinely good at its job, and it still lost.

Sources

  • The Verge: Why the LeapPad couldn’t survive the iPad

item.title: Culture: horror is big business, plus vertical video as a genre
item.description:
The Verge goes deep on horror as big business — the genre's remarkable economics and why it keeps outperforming — alongside a review of George A. Romero's 'Season of the Witch' as a slow-burn feminist occult drama.

Also: Vurt makes the case for vertical video as a genre of its own, not just a format. Whether you buy the argument, it's a more interesting lens than 'phone videos are bad.'

Sources

  • The Verge: George A. Romero’s Season of the Witch is a slow-burn feminist occult drama
  • The Verge: Vurt wants you to look at vertical videos as a genre of their own
  • The Verge: Horror is big business

item.title: Ledger wallet tampering suspected after crypto theft reports
item.description:
The Verge reports suspected tampering with Ledger hardware wallets following a string of crypto thefts.

If confirmed, it's a nightmare scenario for cold-storage holders: the entire point of a hardware wallet is that the device itself is the trust anchor. Expect urgent guidance from Ledger on verifying device authenticity — and a lot of nervous balance-checking across the ecosystem.

Sources

  • The Verge: Ledger wallet tampering suspected after reports of crypto thefts

item.title: Anthropic cuts internal evals from the internet; can AI agents keep their privacy promises?
item.description:
Anthropic is disconnecting its internal model evaluations from the internet, The Verge reports — a notable safety move that also raises a real question about how much real-world behavior lab evals can capture once they're air-gapped.

Separately, The Verge examines whether AI agent makers' privacy promises will survive contact with reality. Agents that can see your inbox, calendar, and files are asking for extraordinary trust; the piece asks what happens when business models and privacy pledges collide.

Sources

  • The Verge: Anthropic is cutting off its internal evaluations from the internet
  • The Verge: AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?

item.title: Reviews: LG's RGB LED TV falls short of OLED; the tiny Telo MT1 charms
item.description:
The Verge reviews LG's new RGB LED TV and finds it good in certain situations — but OLED remains the better buy for most people. New panel tech is genuinely interesting; it just isn't the value play yet, and the review is clear about who should actually consider it.

On wheels, the Telo MT1 electric truck charms reviewers as a big truck trapped in a tiny truck's body. Small footprint, real utility — a compelling formula for city drivers who need hauling without the bulk, if the company can actually ship it.

Sources

  • The Verge: LG's RGB LED TV is good for certain situations, but an OLED is better
  • The Verge: The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck's body

item.title: Culture reads: the techlash goes Hollywood, plus Sunmi, Fjord, and an AI bird feeder
item.description:
The Verge's lighter side leads with how the techlash arrived in Hollywood — the industry that once courted tech money is now making it the villain. A companion podcast deep-dive asks whether Warner Bros. or Skydance comes out of their saga alive.

Also: K-pop star Sunmi on her love of Notion and ear-cleaning videos, the director of Fjord on the 'risky position' of the moderator, and one writer's brief, pest-attracting romance with an AI bird feeder.

Sources

  • The Verge: The techlash has gone Hollywood
  • The Verge: Will Warner Bros. kill Skydance — or will David Ellison kill Warner Bros?
  • The Verge: K-pop star Sunmi loves Notion and ear cleaning videos
  • The Verge: My brief romance with an AI bird feeder
